phy-senses-489.why: Cutaneous nociceptors usually end as unencapsulated branches of sensory axons. They respond to potentially damaging mechanical, thermal or chemical stimuli and transmit signals through A-delta or C fibres.

notes.A: Some touch receptors have specialised capsules, but free nerve endings are also common in skin.
notes.B: Receptive field size varies with receptor type and location. Fingertips often have smaller fields than the trunk.
notes.D: Discriminative touch can ascend in the dorsal columns. Much pain and temperature information travels in the anterolateral system.
notes.E: Cutaneous signals are relayed through several pathways to the brain. The hypothalamus participates in autonomic regulation rather than serving as general sensory storage.

phy-senses-502.why: Pacinian corpuscles have concentric connective-tissue layers surrounding a sensory ending. They lie in deep dermis or subcutaneous tissue and respond best to rapid changes in pressure and high-frequency vibration.

notes.A: Merkel cell–neurite complexes are superficial, slowly adapting receptors for sustained indentation, edges and texture.
notes.C: Free nerve endings are unencapsulated, unlike Pacinian corpuscles. Many mediate pain, temperature or itch.
notes.D: Muscle spindles are stretch receptors within skeletal muscle, where they monitor muscle length and changes in length.
notes.E: Skin stretch is associated particularly with slowly adapting mechanoreceptors. It does not identify the large lamellated pressure and vibration receptor.

phy-senses-510.why: Nociceptors are widespread and numerous in skin. Their branching free endings detect potentially harmful mechanical, thermal and chemical stimuli. Receptor density and the relative numbers vary with the site and the method used to count them.

notes.B: Warmth-sensitive afferents are a specialised subset. They are less widely distributed than the broader population of cutaneous nociceptive endings.
notes.C: Cold spots can outnumber warm spots in many skin regions, but they represent one thermal modality and are not the broadest group listed.
notes.D: The principal proprioceptors are muscle spindles and tendon organs, not the dominant receptors in the skin.
notes.E: Skin stretch is sensed by a subset of cutaneous mechanoreceptors. It does not account for the many free endings that detect noxious stimulation.

phy-senses-540.why: Beta-endorphin is an endogenous opioid peptide that activates opioid receptors and can reduce nociceptive transmission. Natural pain modulation also involves other opioid peptides and descending noradrenergic and serotonergic pathways.

notes.A: Noradrenaline can inhibit nociceptive transmission in descending pathways, but it is not an endogenously produced opioid peptide.
notes.B: Substance P is released by some nociceptive afferents and can help transmit or amplify pain signals in the spinal cord.
notes.C: Dopamine can influence motivation, salience and pain processing. It is not the classic endogenous opioid mediator among these choices.
notes.D: Serotonergic pathways can alter spinal pain transmission, sometimes in either direction. Beta-endorphin provides the direct opioid example here.

phy-senses-546.why: Visceral afferents can respond to excessive stretch, strong contraction, inflammation and chemical irritation. An obstruction can activate several of these mechanisms by increasing wall tension and provoking contractions above the blockage.

notes.A: Excessive distension increases tension in the organ wall and can activate mechanically sensitive visceral afferents.
notes.B: Inflammation releases mediators that can excite or sensitise nociceptive afferents in the wall.
notes.C: Acid can irritate some visceral mucosa and activate chemosensitive afferents. Normal acidic fluid alone does not necessarily cause pain.
notes.D: Strong contractions against an obstruction raise wall tension and can produce intermittent, colicky pain.

phy-senses-547.why: Visceral pain is often diffuse or referred because visceral sensory input is sparse and converges with somatic input in the spinal cord. It can be felt in the midline and may be accompanied by muscle guarding or autonomic responses such as vomiting.

notes.A: Cutaneous sensory input is mapped more precisely than visceral input, so visceral pain is generally harder to localise.
notes.B: Pain from many midline viscera is first perceived near the midline, although referred and localised patterns also occur.
notes.C: Visceral afferent activity can evoke reflex contraction of nearby skeletal muscle, such as abdominal wall guarding.
notes.D: Visceral sensory signals can activate brainstem and autonomic pathways that cause nausea or vomiting.

phy-senses-548.why: Headache can arise when pain-sensitive intracranial vessels or meninges are stimulated. Meningeal inflammation, subarachnoid blood, changes in vascular tone and low cerebrospinal fluid pressure can all contribute in different conditions.

notes.A: Dilatation or other vascular changes can stimulate pain-sensitive structures in some headaches. Vessel calibre is not the only mechanism.
notes.B: Meningeal irritation activates sensory afferents and can cause a severe headache.
notes.C: Blood in the subarachnoid space can irritate the meninges and cause sudden severe head pain.
notes.D: A persistent cerebrospinal fluid leak after lumbar puncture can reduce pressure and produce a positional headache.

phy-senses-549.why: Severe pain can trigger sweating and nausea through autonomic and brainstem pathways. It can also precipitate a vasovagal episode, in which withdrawal of vasoconstrictor tone and increased cardiac vagal activity can lower blood pressure and heart rate.

notes.A: A vasovagal response can decrease vascular resistance in skeletal muscle and other beds, reducing arterial pressure.
notes.B: Increased cardiac vagal drive can slow the heart during a vasovagal episode.
notes.C: Nociceptive and autonomic inputs can activate brainstem circuits that coordinate nausea and vomiting.
notes.D: Sympathetic cholinergic activity can stimulate eccrine sweat glands during severe pain.

phy-senses-490.why: Parasympathetic fibres in the oculomotor pathway stimulate the ciliary muscle for near accommodation. Its contraction reduces zonular tension and lets the lens become more convex, increasing refractive power.

notes.A: Hypermetropia is corrected with a converging lens, which moves the focal point forward onto the retina.
notes.C: The cornea accounts for most of the eye's total refractive power. The lens provides the adjustable component.
notes.D: For distant vision the ciliary muscle is relatively relaxed, allowing the zonules to flatten the lens.
notes.E: Sympathetic activity helps dilate the pupil. The principal active control of near accommodation is parasympathetic.

phy-senses-491.why: Light in one eye normally causes both direct and consensual pupil constriction. Retinal input reaches the pretectal region, which activates parasympathetic pathways from both Edinger–Westphal nuclei to the pupillary sphincters.

notes.A: Normal intraocular pressure is usually substantially above 1.5 mm Hg and commonly lies around 10–21 mm Hg.
notes.C: Near fixation typically produces pupil constriction along with convergence and an increase in lens power.
notes.D: Aqueous humour formation involves diffusion and ultrafiltration, but secretion across the ciliary epithelium accounts for most production.
notes.E: The near response constricts the pupil. Distance fixation does not elicit this same accommodation-associated constriction.

phy-senses-492.why: Cone sensitivity improves first after entering darkness, followed by a slower increase in rod sensitivity as photopigment regenerates. Near-full dark adaptation can take about 30 minutes, depending on prior illumination.

notes.A: Protanopia results from lack of functional long-wavelength cone pigment. Loss of medium-wavelength cone function characterises deuteranopia.
notes.B: In dim light, rod signals dominate and colour discrimination is poor because rods do not distinguish wavelengths by themselves.
notes.D: The central fovea is rod-free. In very dim light, viewing a faint object slightly off-centre can make it easier to see.
notes.E: Photoreceptors are far more numerous than retinal ganglion cells. Many photoreceptors can converge onto downstream retinal pathways.

phy-senses-493.why: The healthy lens maintains more intracellular potassium than sodium and contains abundant soluble crystallins. Reduced glutathione helps protect lens proteins from oxidation. Its depletion is associated with cataract formation.

notes.A: Lens cell transport maintains relatively high potassium and low sodium, helping preserve hydration and transparency.
notes.B: Water-soluble crystallins account for much of the normal lens protein. Cataract can increase the insoluble protein fraction.
notes.C: Reduced glutathione is an important lens antioxidant that protects protein thiol groups.
notes.D: Reduced glutathione can fall in cataract, particularly in the lens nucleus, where oxidative damage accumulates.

phy-senses-494.why: Vitamin A supplies retinal, historically called retinine-1. Its 11-cis form binds opsin in visual pigments. Light changes its configuration and triggers the phototransduction cascade.

notes.A: Somatostatin is a peptide hormone synthesised from amino acids, rather than from vitamin A.
notes.C: Iris colour is mainly determined by melanin and tissue optics. Retinal is a chromophore in photoreceptors.
notes.D: Scotopsin is the rod opsin protein, made from amino acids. Vitamin A supplies the retinal chromophore that binds it.
notes.E: Aqueous humour is produced by the ciliary processes through fluid and solute transport.

phy-senses-498.why: The retina contains rods for sensitive vision in dim light and cones that support detail and colour in brighter conditions. Retinal circuits process the resulting signals before ganglion cells send information to the brain.

notes.B: The retina supplies signals from each eye. Binocular depth perception requires the brain to compare the two views.
notes.C: The ciliary muscles are in the ciliary body, anterior to the retina, and alter lens shape during accommodation.
notes.D: The sclera provides structural protection and helps maintain the shape of the globe. The retina is the sensory lining.
notes.E: Cones provide the initial wavelength signals used for colour, but colour perception also requires comparisons in retinal and central circuits. The retina also supports dim-light vision.

phy-senses-503.why: The sclera is the tough, white, opaque portion of the outer fibrous coat of the eye. It is continuous anteriorly with the transparent cornea.

notes.A: The choroid is a vascular, pigmented layer between retina and sclera. It is not part of the white fibrous coat.
notes.B: The cornea forms the transparent anterior part of the fibrous coat and provides much of the eye's refraction.
notes.C: The retina is the inner neural and photoreceptive layer, rather than the fibrous outer wall.
notes.E: The iris is the pigmented structure that controls pupil size and is part of the vascular coat.

phy-senses-504.why: Myopia is short-sightedness. With accommodation relaxed, rays from a distant object are focused in front of the retina, often because the eye is too long or its refractive power is too strong.

notes.B: In hyperopia, distant rays tend to focus behind the retina when accommodation is relaxed. A converging lens can correct the error.
notes.C: Presbyopia is the age-related loss of accommodation that makes close focusing more difficult.
notes.D: Emmetropia is the state in which distant rays focus on the retina without accommodation.
notes.E: Astigmatism involves unequal refractive power in different meridians and can blur images at multiple distances.

phy-senses-513.why: Rods dominate vision in very dim light and are abundant outside the rod-free central fovea. As rod sensitivity recovers in darkness, faint objects are easier to see slightly off-centre.

notes.A: Cone adaptation occurs early, but rod sensitivity continues to improve for much longer than two or three minutes.
notes.B: Pupil dilation increases retinal illumination, but it is too rapid and too limited to explain the full increase in retinal sensitivity.
notes.C: Both cone and rod photopigment systems adapt. Rods dominate the later phase and provide the greater sensitivity in low light.
notes.D: Red filters reduce stimulation of rods relative to many brighter broad-spectrum exposures, which can help preserve dark adaptation.

phy-senses-515.why: Cones mediate colour vision and high acuity in good light. Central foveal cones are densely packed and have little convergence onto downstream cells, supporting fine spatial detail.

notes.A: The retina contains more rods than cones overall, although the central fovea contains cones and no rods.
notes.C: Rods are more sensitive to dim light. Cones generally need brighter illumination to mediate fine detail and colour.
notes.D: The cone-rich fovea provides the highest spatial acuity of the retina in good light.
notes.E: Both classes use retinal derived from vitamin A, but night blindness from impaired rod function is a characteristic early symptom of deficiency.

phy-senses-517.why: After a transition to darkness, cones adapt relatively quickly and then reach a plateau. Rod sensitivity recovers more slowly and is responsible for the late fall in the threshold for detecting light.

notes.A: The detection threshold falls as sensitivity increases. Progressively dimmer stimuli become visible.
notes.B: Cones contribute mainly to the early phase. Rods provide the greatest sensitivity in the late phase.
notes.D: Bright prior illumination can bleach more visual pigment. It generally delays recovery of full rod sensitivity.
notes.E: Pupil dilation is much faster than full dark adaptation. The slower increase in sensitivity depends on retinal changes.

phy-senses-518.why: A wider pupil lets more light enter and admits more peripheral rays. Those rays are generally less well focused by the optical system, which increases the effect of spherical aberration.

notes.B: Changing aperture alters the bundle of rays entering the eye. It does not itself increase the optical power of the cornea or lens.
notes.C: A wider pupil admits more marginal rays, so spherical aberration generally has a greater rather than smaller effect.
notes.D: Depth of focus decreases when the pupil widens, so modest defocus is more noticeable.
notes.E: The main change is light entry and optical blur. The visual field is chiefly limited by retinal extent and ocular anatomy.

phy-senses-520.why: The near response increases lens curvature, converges the visual axes and constricts the pupils. A smaller pupil increases depth of focus and reduces image blur from spherical and chromatic aberrations, even though wavelength-dependent refraction still exists.

notes.A: Near fixation usually constricts the pupil, reducing the amount of incoming light at the same illumination.
notes.B: The lens becomes more convex as zonular tension falls. The cornea does not normally change curvature as the main accommodation mechanism.
notes.D: Pupil constriction increases depth of focus, allowing a slightly greater range of object distances to appear sharp.
notes.E: Convergence occurs when both eyes turn inward to fixate the same near target.

phy-senses-521.why: Visual acuity measures the ability to resolve fine spatial detail. It is greatest with central foveal vision in adequate light because tightly packed cones and low neural convergence preserve spatial information.

notes.A: Sensitivity to very dim light is a detection threshold, which is different from resolving two nearby details.
notes.B: On a decimal acuity scale, 0.75 represents better resolution than 0.5.
notes.D: Binocular viewing usually provides comparable or somewhat better acuity than monocular viewing when both eyes function well.
notes.E: Common red–green colour vision deficiency can occur with otherwise normal spatial acuity.
